xg_height_width_ratio — 2D xldgeom op

• Data kinds: contour → feature

• Call: fullseye.apply(img, "xg_height_width_ratio", a=0.5, b=0.5) (the 2-D model is one image plus two scalar knobs a,b∈[0,1])

• HALCON equivalent: height_width_ratio_xld (the HALCON reference is a useful guide to its meaning and parameters)

*The figure is the actual output on a synthetic 128×128 input. Left: input, right: output. Point clouds are drawn as a top-down scatter (brightness = z), 1-D series as a line plot, volumes as the maximum-intensity projection along z, videos as the middle frame, complex images as magnitude; return values that are not pictures are shown as the values themselves.*

*Knob a does not change the output (measured: identical at 0.1 / 0.5 / 0.9).*

Stages (the ops that come before → this op, left to right):

▸ xg_height_width_ratio: stages (docs site)

Usage

Axis-aligned bounding-box height/width ratio of the point set.

Merges all contour points (excluding the duplicated end point of closed contours) and returns the ratio of the extent in the row direction h = max(row) - min(row) to the extent in the column direction w = max(col) - min(col), h / w. a, b are unused.

Returns a numpy.float64. 0.0 if there are no points. For w < 1e-12 (all points in the same column = a vertical straight line): 1e6 if h > 1e-12, otherwise 0.0. The upper limit is 1e6. Since it uses the axis-parallel bbox, it is not rotation-invariant (an elongated contour tilted by 45° approaches 1). For rotation-invariant elongation, use xg_elliptic_axis / xg_eccentricity. h, w are ranges of point coordinates (distances between pixel centres), 1 less than a pixel-count-based width. With several contours, it is the ratio of the 1 bbox enclosing them all.
